ri_roadside_wall.blurb: A bouldering wall on Mt. Tom in the forested Arcadia Management Area of southwest Rhode Island, set right beside the trail, so you are at the problems almost as soon as you leave the car. The wall is long and overhanging, with 14 problems running from V0 up to V7. A handful of easy lines make a good warm-up, a few sit around V3 to V5, and the top end is steeper and harder. The rock is granite, with chunky holds on one side and big jugs and slopers in the middle. The upper parts are tall enough to feel like highball territory, and some sections are dirty and want a scrub.

ri_deadwood.blurb: The bouldering and top-rope end of Hemlock Ledges at Beach Pond, on the Rhode Island and Connecticut border. A blocky cave sits at the heart of the area, and a taller overhanging wall rises on its left, roughly 25 to 30 feet high. The 14 problems here span V1 to V11, with a few easy warm-ups and a sizeable group of hard testpieces, so it suits strong boulderers more than beginners. Trees at the top serve as anchors for top-roping. Parts of the wall are not fully cleaned and tend to stay damp, so expect some loose holds and bring a brush.

ut_three_dame_crack_area.blurb: A sunny, south-facing slab in the White Rocks of Utah's West Desert, on the left-hand side of Moon Rock. Of the 14 routes, most are sport lines, with a few trad climbs and one top-rope. Grades stay modest for the most part, from 5.6 to 5.8, with a smaller group of harder 5.10 to 5.12 lines. Some routes are single pitches and others are longer multi-pitch climbs. Descents are mostly by rappel, and a 70 m rope helps because several lines need two-rope rappels. Bring plenty of draws and slings, and a full rack if you plan on the traditional routes. Some of the rock is crumbly.

ut_blacksmith_left.blurb: The left-hand side of Blacksmith Wall, in the Left Hand Fork of Blacksmith Fork Canyon in Cache Valley, northern Utah. This is a steep, streaked wall holding 14 sport routes, all of them 5.12 or 5.13, so it is a destination for experienced climbers rather than a place to learn. Several lines have extensions and link-ups. The rock is decent, but the approach is loose and a little crusty, and you have to cross the river on foot to get to the wall from the road.

ut_hobbit_caves.blurb: A small, pleasant wall in Right Hand Fork, a side canyon of Logan Canyon in Cache Valley. It holds 14 climbs, nearly all sport routes plus one mixed line and one top-rope. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, so it works for intermediate climbers looking for a short day. A small stream runs through, there are caves to poke around in, and the scenery is a draw. You cross the river by a plank bridge to reach the main wall. Litter and broken glass have been a problem, so bring a bag and pack some out.

ut_hard_wall.blurb: A compact, steep limestone wall in American Fork Canyon, in the southern Wasatch, a short walk from the Hell area. It is a small overhanging cave with 14 short sport routes, from 5.8 up to 5.13, though most sit at 5.11 and 5.12, so the rock is best suited to climbers working harder grades. The wall faces southeast and catches sun through the morning and into mid-afternoon, which makes it a decent choice on cold, clear days. The rock quality is only fair. The trail up is steep and loose, and the cave is the obvious feature on the left once you reach the gully.

ut_kermits_wall.blurb: A long, slabby wall in Little Cottonwood Canyon, just left of the Schoolroom and about a mile and a quarter up the canyon road from the Gate Buttress lot. A distinct dihedral separates the lower wall from the upper one. The 14 climbs are mostly trad, with some bolted sport lines, a top-rope and an aid problem. Grades are centred on 5.10, with a scattering of easier lines and a few 5.11 and 5.12 routes. Nice cracks split the face, and the thin cracks and bolted lines suit climbers who like technical, sustained movement on a slab.
